schools.summary: Matthew Henry turns the safe return into a meditation on distinguishing mercy: Jehoshaphat fared better than he expected, than he deserved, and than Ahab who came home slain, for God owns the way of the righteous.
Ellicott hears in 'in peace' (whole, sound, unhurt) a deliberate contrast with the fate of Ahab.
Clarke reads 'in peace' as in safety, from a danger only God's especial mercy could have brought him through, and sketches the chapter to come.
Gill fixes the circumstance: returned from Ramoth-gilead after Ahab was slain.

Ellicott gives Jehu's record (against Asa, Baasha), parses 'shouldest thou help' as an infinitive with 'the ungodly' emphatic, and reads the threatened wrath as fulfilled in Jehoshaphat's later invasion, shipwreck, and evil posterity; Keil sets the rebuke as the turn back to reform.

Clarke reads the wrath as 'thou deservest to be punished' and widens it to all alliances with the ungodly; Wesley traces the chastisement through the Moabite invasion, Jehoram's fratricide, and Jehu's slaughter of the grandchildren.
Gill marks the courage of the seer's line: son of the Hanani whom Asa imprisoned, yet undeterred from reproving a king.

outliers.note: Broadens the rebuke into a standing rule: the wrath of God rests upon all alliances his people form with the ungodly, whether social, matrimonial, commercial, or political.

themes: an unequal yoke with the ungodly

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in 'nevertheless' a reprieve from destruction, renders 'taken away the groves' as 'consumed the Asherahs,' and reads 'prepared thine heart' as directing it Godward — the opposite of Rehoboam.
Gill reads the 'good things' as inward graces — grace, righteousness, holiness, faith, love, zeal — from which good works spring.
Wesley: the good marks of an honest heart, which God regards more than this one error; he will chasten but not utterly destroy.

themes: the good things found in the king
a heart prepared to seek God

schools.summary: Keil binds the clauses (dwelt, then went forth again) from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim; Ellicott ties the circuit to the earlier teaching commission and reads 'brought them back' as reclaiming the people from a fused Baal-and-Jehovah worship.

Clarke marks the shrunken kingdom's bounds and the king's personal inspection of justice; Wesley: he reclaimed the revolted by counsel, example, and the Levites' instruction, doubly obliged after his own bad example.
Gill: Jehoshaphat dwelt at Jerusalem and went no more to Samaria, attending to his own affairs.

debates.question: Did Jehoshaphat conduct the visitation in person or through representatives?

sides.position: in person, going through all his territories to examine everything himself
not necessarily in person, but by his accredited representatives

outliers.note: Reads 'brought them back unto the LORD' against the tendency of the age to fuse the worship of Jehovah with the Canaanite cult of Baal, citing modern scholarship on the two religions' assimilation.

schools.summary: Keil sets the judges in the fenced cities as centres of communication, 'city by city' per Deut. 16:18; Ellicott glosses 'he set' as appointed or stationed, the judges being Levites, priests, and family chiefs.
Matthew Henry reads the judges as the sequel to the preachers of 2 Chron. 17 — a settled magistracy to execute the law and be a terror to evil-doers, the old courts new-modelled.
Gill: inferior courts in every city, ordained by David but neglected, now restored.

Keil: the judges act in the name and will of the LORD, to whom judgment belongs; Ellicott calls them Jehovah's vicegerents, reads 'with you in the judgment' as God present at sentencing (Ps. 82), and notes 'Jehoshaphat' means 'Jehovah judgeth.'
Clarke: judges stand in the place of God and will be judged for their judgments; Wesley reads God 'with you' both to observe your conduct and to defend you against the enemies justice provokes.
Matthew Henry gathers three motives from God: the commission is his, his eye is on the court, and he is the pattern of justice without iniquity or respect of persons.
Gill: judge righteous judgment by the law of God, without partiality or respect of persons.

themes: judging in the room of God
not for man but for the LORD

schools.summary: Ellicott parses 'wherefore' as 'and,' 'take heed and do' as a hendiadys, and 'iniquity' as want of equity, adding the bribe-prohibition of Deut. 16:19; Keil grounds the fear of the LORD on God's own impartial, incorruptible character.
Wesley: those in God's stead, doing his work and answerable to him, must imitate God in his justice.
Matthew Henry: God is the great example of justice — no iniquity, bribery, or respect of persons — whom magistrates, called gods, must resemble.
Gill: act with the fear of the LORD ever before your eyes and upon your hearts.

themes: the fear of the LORD upon the bench
no iniquity or respect of persons
judging like the God you judge for

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the court in its legal history (Exod. 18; David's Levite-judges of 1 Chron. 23; the appeal court of Deut. 17), distinguishing the LORD's matters from civil 'controversies,' and reads the last clause as the commission's return.
Clarke doubts the received 'when they returned,' emending to 'the inhabitants of Jerusalem'; Wesley reads it of Jehoshaphat's homecoming and leaves open whether there was one court or two.
Gill: a great court of both ecclesiastics and political persons, since causes of both sorts came before it.
Matthew Henry: the appeal court under the king's eye, of learned priests and Levites and the chief of the fathers.

debates.question: How should the last clause, 'when they returned to Jerusalem,' be read?

sides.position: emend the word to 'the inhabitants,' i.e. 'for the controversies of the inhabitants of Jerusalem' (with Vulgate and LXX)
keep 'they returned to Jerusalem' as a note of time — the return of the royal commission of v.4

debates.question: Was it a single court or two distinct benches?

sides.position: two distinct jurisdictions, ecclesiastical and civil
uncertain whether one Sanhedrin or two separate courts

themes: a textual crux in the last clause

schools.summary: Ellicott shows the high court charged exactly as the country judges were (vv.6-7), 'perfect heart' meaning integrity; Keil notes 'thus shall ye do' defers its content to v.10, the following conjunction being explicative.
Matthew Henry: they must act from a good principle, in the fear of the LORD, and so act faithfully and with a perfect upright heart.
Gill: the charge is addressed to the members of the court at Jerusalem.

themes: the charge repeated to the high court
fear, fidelity, and a perfect heart
the same terms for great and small

schools.summary: Ellicott defines the appellate causes — 'between blood and blood' (murder or manslaughter, Deut. 17:8) and questions of legal interpretation — and reads 'warn them' as 'instruct them,' the miscarriage of justice implicating the whole people in guilt; Keil concurs on the categories.

Clarke sorts the two heads of cases; Wesley, with Henry, notes that since the revolt only Hebron's city of refuge remained to Judah, so homicide trials fell to Jerusalem, and reads 'warn' as admonishing offender and others for the future.
Matthew Henry: 'This do, and ye shall not trespass' means those in power contract guilt if they do not use it to restrain sin — 'you trespass if you do not keep them from trespassing.'
Gill: whatever causes, sacred or civil, came up by appeal from the inferior courts.

themes: cities of refuge lost to the north
the judge's duty to teach and warn

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Amariah the High Priest (probably the man fifth from Zadok) as head in the LORD's matters and Zebadiah the nagid as head in civil causes, the Levites as scribes, and reads 'the LORD be with the good' as a prayer in the chronicler's style.
Clarke sets out the two-fold jurisdiction, ecclesiastical under Amariah and civil under Zebadiah, insisting the things of God and of the king should never be confounded.

Matthew Henry sees in the two presidents diversities of gifts from one Spirit — men of the LORD's matters and of the king's, both needful — and hears in 'deal courageously' a call to fearless duty under God's protection.
Gill: Amariah presided in all things sacred, present to advise and direct according to the statutes.

themes: the two presidents of the court
deal courageously — the LORD with the good
